Neonatal New Zealand sea lions emerge at a relatively large size compared to other otariids, with pups measuring approximately 75 centimeters [Lb = approximately 75 centimeters] in total length at birth. This substantial neonatal length is complemented by a birth mass of about 11 kilograms [Wwb = about 11 kilograms], reflecting the significant maternal investment typical of this species. The energetic demands of gestation are considerable, and under the stable core body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C] that characterizes this pinniped, the gestation period extends for 365 days [tg = 365 days]. This extended pregnancy, nearly identical to that of the closely related Australian sea lion, ensures that pups are born in a well-developed, precocial state during the austral summer, a timing that aligns with peak prey availability for nursing females. The substantial size at birth is thought to confer a survival advantage during the first few weeks, when pups must rapidly gain mass and develop thermoregulatory independence on crowded breeding beaches. Field records consistently note that these neonatal dimensions are among the largest recorded for any otariid species relative to maternal body size.

Sexual dimorphism in the New Zealand sea lion is pronounced and becomes evident as individuals approach reproductive maturity. Adult females attain a total body length of approximately 200 centimeters [Li = approximately 200 centimeters], with reported values typically falling within a range of 180 to 200 centimeters. In stark contrast, adult males are considerably larger, reaching total lengths of up to 350 centimeters [Li = up to 350 centimeters], though field measurements commonly range from 240 to 350 centimeters in dominant breeding bulls. This disparity in linear dimensions is mirrored in body mass, where the ultimate wet weight for females stabilizes around 160 kilograms [Wwi = around 160 kilograms], while males can achieve an ultimate wet weight of 450 kilograms [Wwi = 450 kilograms]. Substantial variation exists within each sex, with some females recorded as low as 90 kilograms and large territorial males occasionally exceeding 450 kilograms. This extreme dimorphism is indicative of intense polygynous breeding systems, where male reproductive success is tightly linked to the ability to defend and monopolize access to females on rookeries.

The timeline of reproductive development in female New Zealand sea lions unfolds over several years before they contribute to the breeding population. Under the standard physiological temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], the time since birth at puberty for females is approximately 2,030 days [tp = approximately 2,030 days], which corresponds to roughly 5.6 years of age. This relatively late onset of sexual maturity is typical of long-lived marine mammals and is thought to be a consequence of the extended period required to acquire the body size and energy reserves necessary for successful gestation and lactation. The extended juvenile period in both sexes allows for extensive learning of foraging techniques and navigation of the complex marine environment surrounding the subantarctic breeding islands.

The transition from nutritional dependence to independent foraging is a critical developmental milestone for young New Zealand sea lions. Weaning occurs at an average of 213 days after birth [tx = 213 days after birth], a duration that is maintained under the species’ characteristic body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. This protracted nursing period, lasting approximately seven months, is among the longest observed in otariid seals and reflects the challenging, energy-poor waters of the Southern Ocean where pups must eventually forage. During this time, pups gradually shift from a diet of milk to solid prey, learning critical hunting skills from their mothers through observation and experimentation. Following weaning, juveniles face a period of elevated mortality risk as they must independently locate sufficient prey resources. The timing of weaning is carefully aligned with seasonal peaks in local prey abundance, such as the availability of arrow squid and juvenile hoki, which helps to buffer the energetic challenges of this life-history transition.

Longevity in the New Zealand sea lion is considerable, with the species’ maximum lifespan estimated at 26 years [am = 26 years] under the stable core temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. A captive or field record calculated as 9,490 days [am = 9,490 days] places the species among the longer-lived otariids, comparable to the Steller sea lion at a temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. Despite this potential, realized lifespans in the wild are often shorter due to high rates of bycatch in trawl fisheries, disease outbreaks, and stochastic environmental events that reduce prey availability. The maximum reproductive rate for this species is approximately one pup per year [Ri = approximately one pup per year], a low fecundity that is characteristic of capital-breeding pinnipeds that invest heavily in each offspring. This single-pup annual output [Ri = single-pup annual output] is achieved under the species’ physiological temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C] and is a direct consequence of the extended gestation and lactation periods. Such a slow reproductive schedule makes the New Zealand sea lion particularly vulnerable to population declines, as even modest increases in adult mortality can have disproportionately large effects on population growth rates. Conservation efforts therefore prioritize the protection of breeding females and their critical foraging grounds.
